design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, four-arm crossover study in a hospital clinical research centre (San Francisco General Hospital): placebo, ethanol, GHB and ethanol plus GHB in random order (4 by 4 Latin square), four 24-hour visits at least 2 days apart, after an overnight fast. Each person received ethanol 0.3 g/kg (vodka in juice) or placebo juice at about 8:00, then 15 minutes later GHB 50 mg/kg (sodium oxybate, Xyrem) or placebo with a second ethanol 0.3 g/kg or placebo. Heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate and skin temperature were recorded at intervals for 4 hours, oxygen saturation by continuous pulse oximetry for 4 hours, and blood and urine sampled for 24 hours for GHB and ethanol concentrations. 22 adults enrolled and 16 completed all four visits and were analysed. Subjective effects, cognitive testing and differences by sex and race are to be reported separately and are not in this paper.
can_establish: In 16 healthy, light-drinking adults in a hospital research unit, after a single GHB dose and a single ethanol dose given alone or together: whether mean oxygen saturation, blood pressure, heart rate and skin temperature differed between the four conditions, how often vomiting and brief low blood pressure occurred, and whether ethanol changed GHB blood levels by an amount large enough to detect with 16 people (about 25%).
cannot_establish: Whether the combination causes respiratory failure, loss of consciousness or death in real-life use (mean oxygen saturation fell by about 2 percentage points at most; no event needed treatment; sedation, breathing rate and cognitive effects are not reported in this paper); effects at higher or unknown doses, with other drugs, or in people with lung disease; effects of GBL or 1,4-butanediol; whether the combined fall is greater than the sum of the single-drug falls (no interaction test is reported); and pharmacokinetic effects smaller than about 25%.

sample.recruitment: Not described beyond “recruited” (the Acknowledgments thank a staff member for recruitment); potential participants were not selected by race or ethnicity (Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy adults aged 21 to 45 by history, physical examination and screening laboratory tests. Excluded: any significant medical history, pregnancy or obesity; people who used illicit drugs; people taking prescription drugs other than oral contraceptives; more than light alcohol use (more than 3 drinks a week) or GHB use (more than twice in the previous 6 months).
sample.demographics: 16 completers: 7 men and 9 women, aged 22 to 34; weight 47.9 to 83.0 kg (mean 66.2); height 146 to 183 cm (mean 169); 7 white (44%), 6 Asian or Pacific Islander (38%), 1 Latino (6%), 2 of multiple ethnicities (12%).
sample.attrition: 6 of 22 (27%) withdrew: 1 man after his first visit (lost interest) and 5 women (1 lost interest, 2 poor intravenous access, 2 protocol violations). The 16 completers are the minimum the power calculation required. No adverse event led to withdrawal or needed medical treatment. The completers' distribution across the four Latin-square sequences is not given.
sample.selection_effects: Healthy, light-drinking adults with almost no prior GHB use who agreed to take GHB and ethanol in a research unit, mostly women, tested supine and monitored. They are unlike people who present to emergency departments after taking GHB with alcohol, who may have taken higher or unknown amounts, other drugs, or both, in uncontrolled settings.

exposure.measurement: Study-administered. Pharmaceutical sodium oxybate (Xyrem, supplied by its manufacturer) and vodka in orange or cranberry juice, with placebo juice. Plasma GHB by a gas chromatography-mass spectrometry method (limit of quantitation 5 µg/mL, because lower values are in the range of the body's own GHB) and blood ethanol by an enzymatic assay.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: a single oral GHB dose of 50 mg/kg, which the authors describe as comparable to doses used to treat narcolepsy, with or without ethanol 0.3 g/kg by mouth before and 0.3 g/kg by mouth together with the GHB 15 minutes later (0.6 g/kg in all), after an overnight fast. Average peak blood ethanol was 70.7 mg/dL alone and 76.6 mg/dL with GHB, against about 50 mg/dL projected (Table 2).
exposure.polysubstance: People using illicit or prescription drugs were excluded; alcohol was not allowed for 3 days before each visit and caffeine, tobacco and food were withheld overnight. No drug screen is mentioned.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: No alcohol for 3 days before each study day and an overnight fast from food, caffeine and tobacco, by instruction; not verified.

comparison.controls: Within-person: each of the 16 had placebo, ethanol alone, GHB alone and both. The study is described as double-blind, but the paper does not say how the placebo for GHB was matched or whether blinding was checked.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (within-person). Order by 4 by 4 Latin square; visits at least 2 days apart.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not reported: sleep before each visit, menstrual cycle phase, use of oral contraceptives (allowed), usual alcohol intake within the light range, and tolerance. Weight-based dosing means men and women, who differ in body water and fat, received different absolute amounts.

outcomes.instruments: Dinamap automated blood pressure; heart rate; skin temperature; respiratory rate (recorded, not reported); oxygen saturation by continuous pulse oximetry for 4 hours (device and averaging not described); plasma GHB and blood ethanol for pharmacokinetics; adverse events (Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: No clinical threshold is applied and no baseline oxygen saturation, lowest individual value or number of people below any threshold is reported. The authors call the 2% change modest in absolute terms.
outcomes.operationalization: Respiratory effect is the change in pulse oximetry saturation from a pre-dose baseline (the paper defines baseline for hemodynamic variables as the average of readings at 0, 15 and 30 minutes before dosing and does not say so separately for oxygen saturation), shown as the maximum mean change and the 0 to 4 hour area under the change curve. Breathing rate, carbon dioxide and sedation are not outcomes in this paper.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None stated: five pharmacodynamic outcomes (systolic and diastolic blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, skin temperature) compared pairwise across four conditions, and 11 pharmacokinetic parameters (7 for GHB, 4 for ethanol) compared by paired t tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind is stated in the abstract and Methods; automated measurements. Not stated whether the people reading the oximeter or analysing the data knew the condition; sedation from the drugs would be visible to staff.

analysis.effect_sizes: Oxygen saturation: all three active conditions lower than placebo; the combination gave the greatest drop, with a maximal mean change of −2.12 ± 0.34 percentage points at 90 minutes, greater than placebo (P < 0.0001), GHB alone (P = 0.027) and ethanol alone (P = 0.013); all active conditions stayed significantly below baseline for the 4 hours of monitoring (Results › Oxygen Saturation, 1st paragraph). Read by eye from Figure 2 (approximate, mean change from baseline in percentage points): at 90 minutes, combination about −2.2, GHB alone about −1.6, ethanol alone about −0.75, placebo about −0.6; the placebo curve itself drifts down by roughly 0.4 to 0.9 over the 4 hours. No interaction contrast, confidence interval or baseline saturation is given. Blood pressure and heart rate: ethanol alone lowered systolic pressure (peak −15.7 ± 3.0 mm Hg at 105 minutes, P = 0.0006 against GHB alone) and raised heart rate (peak +13.5 ± 2.3 beats per minute at 45 minutes, P = 0.006 against placebo); GHB alone had no significant effect and the combination was not greater than ethanol alone; diastolic pressure with the combination fell by up to 16.9 ± 2.5 mm Hg (P = 0.012 against placebo). Skin temperature rose by up to 2.9 ± 0.7 °F with the combination (P < 0.001 against placebo, P = 0.028 against ethanol alone). Adverse events: vomiting on 8 study days (combination 6, GHB alone 1, ethanol alone 1) and 2 brief asymptomatic drops in systolic pressure to 71 to 73 mm Hg after the combination; no test. Pharmacokinetics of GHB (mean ± SD, alone against with ethanol; Table 1, all P > 0.05 by paired t test): peak 72.6 ± 16.2 against 84.0 ± 25.8 µg/mL (+16%); half-life 51.8 ± 21.3 against 67.0 ± 48.4 minutes (+29%); area under the curve 9,330 ± 3,390 against 11,360 ± 4,796 µg·min/mL; clearance 6.2 ± 2.7 against 5.0 ± 2.4 mL/min/kg. Editors' calculation: area under the curve +22% and clearance −19%, no intervals given. Ethanol (Table 2, all P > 0.05): peak 70.7 ± 11.6 against 76.6 ± 13.3 mg/dL; area under the curve 19,810 ± 5,342 against 18,840 ± 6,450 mg·min/dL.
analysis.covariates: A random subject effect and fixed effects for treatment and all two-way interactions in a mixed-effects regression of the area under the change curve; no adjustment for sex, weight or order.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration number or analysis plan is given. The paper states that the primary aim was the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interaction between the two drugs, and that other outcomes will be reported separately.
analysis.selective_reporting: Respiratory rate was recorded but is not reported. Subjective effects, cognitive tests and sex and race differences are held for other papers, so the outcomes closest to sedation and consciousness are not in this one. The headline oxygen saturation figure is a change from baseline, not from placebo.
analysis.power: Powered for a 25% difference in GHB clearance with ethanol (80% power, 2-sided 0.05, 16 completers). The observed clearance difference was about 19%, and the half-life, peak and area-under-the-curve differences were 29%, 16% and 22%: smaller than the study was designed to detect, so “not statistically significant” cannot be read as “no interaction”. No power calculation for oxygen saturation or adverse events.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 16 healthy, light-drinking adults given a single moderate GHB dose and a moderate ethanol dose in a research unit, mean oxygen saturation fell by about 2 percentage points at most when the two were taken together, more than with GHB alone (P = 0.027) or ethanol alone (P = 0.013); vomiting happened on 6 of 8 days with vomiting after the combination; two brief asymptomatic drops in systolic blood pressure occurred after it; blood pressure and heart rate changes came from ethanol. GHB blood levels were about 16% higher at peak and the half-life about 29% longer with ethanol, but 16 people could not detect differences of that size.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that GHB plus ethanol “resulted in more adverse effects” including gastrointestinal disturbance, hypotension and decreased oxygen saturation, “but only minimal pharmacokinetic interactions”. The Discussion says the combination “intensifies respiratory depression, which may explain” some of the severe toxicity and deaths seen in recreational use (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Gaps: (1) respiratory depression is inferred from a fall of about 2 percentage points in pulse oximetry with no breathing rate, carbon dioxide or ventilation data (breathing rate was recorded but not reported), and the authors themselves call the change modest; (2) “more adverse effects” rests on 6 against 1 and 1 vomiting days and 2 brief hypotension episodes in 16 people, untested; (3) “minimal” pharmacokinetic interaction rests on non-significance in a study powered for a 25% change in clearance, where every estimate moves the same way; (4) the step from a single modest dose in healthy supine volunteers to deaths in recreational use is not tested by this design; (5) whether the effect of the two together exceeds the sum of their separate effects is not examined.

timeline.event: Mattila et al.: a study of GHB with low-dose ethanol reported significantly impaired reaction time with the combination (as described by Thai et al.; not read).
Chin et al.: clinical course of GHB overdose in 88 emergency department patients, 11 intubated and 21 with raised arterial carbon dioxide (as described by Thai et al.; not read).
Van Sassenbroeck et al.: in rats, ethanol did not change GHB blood levels or area under the curve but prolonged sleeping time (as described by Thai et al.; not read).
This study: the first human pharmacokinetic and hemodynamic study of the combination, by the authors' account.

Galicia (Toxicol Lett), Euro-DEN Plus Registry (22 emergency departments in 14 European countries, 18 of which contributed cases), 609 patients with acute toxicity from GHB or GBL alone (183) or with ethanol (426) and no other drug: reduced consciousness (Glasgow Coma Score below 13) 58.9% with ethanol against 49.1% without (P = 0.034), more admissions to critical care among those admitted (55.3% against 22.4%), no detectable difference in slow breathing or intubation, and two deaths, both with ethanol. Read for this library from the accepted manuscript: a different design (observational, univariable), population and outcomes, and not a repeat of this crossover.

replication.where_it_stands: No repeat of this crossover design in humans was identified in the paper's reference list. The direction (more central nervous system depression with the combination) is echoed in one emergency department registry analysis read for this library (Galicia, 2019), which measured consciousness, treatment and critical care rather than oxygen saturation, did not adjust for the GHB amount taken or for centre, and found no detectable difference in slow breathing or intubation. Neither study repeats the other.

funding.funder: US National Institute on Drug Abuse grants (DA 14935, DA12393), a clinical pharmacology training grant and a General Clinical Research Center award from the National Institutes of Health. The GHB used (Xyrem) was provided by its manufacturer, Orphan Medical Company; the paper does not state whether the manufacturer had any role in the study.
funding.declared_conflicts: Two authors have given paid medicolegal consultation in cases involving GHB; the other two declare none.
funding.affiliations_note: The affiliation list was collapsed on the page and was not extracted; the ethics committee and the research centre are at the University of California, San Francisco and San Francisco General Hospital. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A larger randomized crossover study, powered for the interaction between the two drugs on oxygen saturation and breathing (with respiratory rate, carbon dioxide and sedation reported as well), at several GHB and ethanol levels that can safely be given, reporting the interaction contrast with its interval and the lowest individual values; together with emergency department and poison-centre series that record coma, intubation and intensive-care admission with and without ethanol and adjust for the GHB amount taken, which only observational data can reach.

domains.note: Random order by a 4 by 4 Latin square, but how sequences were generated and concealed is not described, and the 16 completers' spread across sequences is not given. Within-person contrasts remove between-person confounding.
At least 2 days between visits, long after GHB (half-life about an hour) and ethanol are cleared; order balanced by the Latin square. No period effect is reported.

Described as double-blind, but the paper does not say how GHB (a salty-tasting solution) and ethanol were matched by placebo or whether blinding was checked, and both drugs cause effects participants and staff can notice. Two women withdrew for protocol violations.

6 of 22 (27%) did not complete, 5 of them women, for reasons that appear unrelated to the outcome (loss of interest, poor intravenous access) but with no analysis of enrolled participants; the 16 completers are the minimum the power calculation required.

Continuous pulse oximetry is automated, but the device, its accuracy, the averaging and the baseline values are not described, the change measured is small (about 2 points), and breathing rate was recorded but not reported.

No registration or analysis plan; respiratory rate not reported; sedation, cognitive and subjective outcomes deferred to other papers; many pairwise tests without correction; the headline saturation change is from baseline, not from placebo, and no interaction contrast is given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The randomized, placebo-controlled within-person design protects the comparisons between conditions against confounding, and the exposure was administered under control; but 5 of 6 domains raise some concerns (unreported blinding method, a 27% dropout, incomplete outcome reporting and no interaction test), none judged high because the outcome is automated and the dropouts seem unrelated to it. The source may be cited for the direction and rough size of the mean oxygen saturation change under these conditions and for the vomiting and blood pressure observations. It may not be cited for the size of the risk to breathing or consciousness in real use, for whether the combined effect exceeds the sum of the single effects, or for a lack of pharmacokinetic interaction.

key_findings.finding: 22 healthy adults aged 21 to 45 enrolled; 16 completed (7 men, 9 women, aged 22 to 34, mean weight 66.2 kg). Eligible people used alcohol lightly (no more than 3 drinks a week) and had taken GHB no more than twice in the previous 6 months; people who used illicit or prescription drugs (other than oral contraceptives) were excluded. 6 withdrew (1 man, 5 women).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 1st paragraph; Results › Subject Characteristics, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Randomized, double-blind, four-arm crossover (4 by 4 Latin square) with placebo, ethanol, GHB and the combination at four 24-hour visits at least 2 days apart: ethanol 0.3 g/kg or placebo at about 8:00, then 15 minutes later GHB 50 mg/kg (Xyrem) or placebo plus a second ethanol 0.3 g/kg or placebo; supine for 3 hours.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Monitoring: heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate and skin temperature at 30 and 15 minutes before dosing, at dosing, every 15 minutes for 2 hours and every 30 minutes for the next 2 hours; oxygen saturation by continuous pulse oximetry for 4 hours; blood at 15, 30, 45, 60 and 90 minutes and 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 12 and 24 hours; urine to 24 hours.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Respiratory rate is listed here but no result for it appears; the blood pressure and heart rate area-under-the-curve window (0 to 6 hours) and the statement that ethanol lowered systolic pressure for 5 hours are longer than the 4-hour schedule given (reporting issue 4).

key_findings.finding: Statistics: powered to detect a 25% difference in GHB clearance caused by ethanol (16 completers, 80% power, 2-sided 0.05); pharmacokinetic parameters by paired t tests; pharmacodynamic data by mixed-effects regression with treatment, all two-way interactions and a random subject effect, with pairwise comparisons; baseline for blood pressure and heart rate was the average of readings at 0, 15 and 30 minutes before dosing; area under the change curve for oxygen saturation over 0 to 4 hours and for heart rate and blood pressure over 0 to 6 hours.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical and Data Analysis, 1st paragraph; Pharmacokinetic Analysis, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Oxygen saturation fell with all three active conditions relative to placebo. The combination gave the largest drop: maximal mean change −2.12 ± 0.34 percentage points at 90 minutes, greater than placebo (P < 0.0001), GHB alone (P = 0.027) and ethanol alone (P = 0.013); saturation stayed significantly below baseline for the 4 hours of monitoring with all three active conditions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamics › Oxygen Saturation, 1st paragraph; Abstract (Results)
key_findings.note: The −2.12 is the change from each person's baseline, not from placebo; Figure 2 shows the placebo curve itself below baseline.

key_findings.finding: Figure 2 (mean change in percentage points from baseline over 240 minutes, with 95% confidence intervals), read by eye and approximate: combination near −0.75 at 15 minutes, −1.6 at 30 to 45 minutes, about −2.2 at 90 minutes, −2.0 at 105 and 150 minutes, and about −1.4 to −1.6 from 180 to 240 minutes; GHB alone about −1.6 at 90 minutes and −1.5 at 150 to 240 minutes; ethanol alone between about −0.4 and −1.2; placebo between about +0.4 at 15 minutes and −0.9 at 210 minutes. The paper reports no interaction contrast; from the plot, the combined fall looks about the size of the GHB-alone fall plus a small ethanol fall.
key_findings.note: Approximate reading; the paper gives numbers only for the combination's maximum.

key_findings.finding: Adverse events: vomiting on 8 study days (6 with the combination, 1 with GHB alone, 1 with ethanol alone) and 2 episodes of brief asymptomatic hypotension (systolic 71 to 73 mm Hg, under 15 minutes) after the combination; none needed treatment and all resolved by themselves; no event led to withdrawal.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse Events, 1st paragraph; Subject Characteristics, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Blood pressure and heart rate: ethanol lowered systolic pressure for 5 hours (peak −15.7 ± 3.0 mm Hg at 105 minutes, P = 0.0006 against GHB alone) and diastolic pressure (peak −16.9 ± 2.5 mm Hg 2 hours after the combination, P = 0.012 against placebo) and raised heart rate (peak +13.5 ± 2.3 beats per minute at 45 minutes, P = 0.006 against placebo); GHB alone had no significant effect on either, and the combination was not greater than ethanol alone. Skin temperature rose by up to 2.9 ± 0.7 °F with the combination (P < 0.001 against placebo, P = 0.028 against ethanol alone) in the first hour.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamics › Blood Pressure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Heart Rate, 1st paragraph; Skin Temperature, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Pharmacokinetics (Tables 1 and 2; mean ± SD, n = 16; all differences P > 0.05): GHB peak 72.6 ± 16.2 alone against 84.0 ± 25.8 µg/mL with ethanol; half-life 51.8 ± 21.3 against 67.0 ± 48.4 minutes; area under the curve 9,330 ± 3,390 against 11,360 ± 4,796 µg·min/mL; clearance 6.2 ± 2.7 against 5.0 ± 2.4 mL/min/kg; renal clearance and the share of the dose recovered in urine (about 5%) unchanged. Ethanol peak 70.7 ± 11.6 alone against 76.6 ± 13.3 mg/dL with GHB (against about 50 mg/dL projected); rate of blood ethanol decline 0.24 ± 0.07 against 0.26 ± 0.08 mg/dL per minute.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the table means: GHB area under the curve +22%, clearance −19%.

key_findings.finding: Authors' reading: the combination “was found to have increased respiratory depressant effects”; a fall of about 2% in saturation is modest in absolute terms but could matter if a person has taken other drugs that slow breathing or has lung disease; intensified respiratory depression “may explain some of the severe toxicity and deaths reported”. They add that a small ethanol effect on GHB clearance or bioavailability could matter more at higher GHB doses such as unintentional overdoses.
Funding: US National Institute on Drug Abuse and National Institutes of Health grants; Xyrem provided by its manufacturer; two authors have been paid medicolegal consultants in GHB cases.
key_findings.locator: Acknowledgments; Conflict of Interest Statement (end matter)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says blood pressure and heart rate effects were significant “compared with baseline”, but the Results give the P values against GHB alone (systolic pressure, P = 0.0006) and against placebo (heart rate, P = 0.006; diastolic pressure, P = 0.012).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which comparison each P value belongs to differs between the abstract and the Results; the Results wording should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: The headline oxygen saturation change (−2.1%, “P < 0.0001 vs placebo”) is the change from baseline with the combination, not a difference from placebo. In Figure 2 the placebo curve is itself below baseline for most of the 4 hours (by eye, about 0.4 to 0.9 points), and the paper gives no baseline saturation, lowest individual value or number of people under any threshold.
reporting_issues.consequence: The fall attributable to the drugs is smaller than the headline (by eye, about 1.5 points at 90 minutes for the combination against placebo), and how close any person came to a clinically relevant level cannot be told.

reporting_issues.issue: Respiratory rate was recorded (Methods) but no result for it is reported. Subjective effects, cognitive testing and effects by sex and race are said to be reported separately.
reporting_issues.consequence: The only breathing outcome reported is pulse oximetry, and nothing about sedation or consciousness is in this paper, though the abstract and Discussion speak of respiratory depression and sedative effects.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods give vital-sign recording every 15 minutes for 2 hours and every 30 minutes for the next 2 hours (4 hours), but the analysis window for heart rate and blood pressure is 0 to 6 hours and the Results say ethanol lowered systolic pressure “for 5 hours”.
reporting_issues.consequence: The monitoring schedule for blood pressure and heart rate is incompletely described; the results beyond 4 hours cannot be traced to a stated measurement schedule.

reporting_issues.issue: The study was powered to detect a 25% change in GHB clearance. The observed differences with ethanol (peak +16%, half-life +29%, area under the curve about +22% and clearance about −19% by editors' calculation) were each “not significant”, no confidence intervals are given, and the abstract concludes that only “minimal” pharmacokinetic interactions were observed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Absence of statistical significance in 16 people is not evidence of no interaction; all four estimates point to more GHB exposure with ethanol, and an effect of 20% to 30% could not be excluded.

reporting_issues.issue: The mixed-effects model is described as including all two-way interactions, but no interaction estimate (whether the combined effect exceeds the sum of the single effects) is reported; the conclusions rest on pairwise comparisons only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper cannot be cited for synergy or for additivity; “more than either alone” is shown, “more than their sum” is not tested.

reporting_issues.issue: The ethanol dose was projected to give blood levels near 50 mg/dL; the average peak was 70.7 mg/dL alone and 76.6 mg/dL with GHB (Table 2). The Methods do not discuss the difference.
reporting_issues.consequence: The average peak was roughly 40% to 55% above the projection (editors' calculation), so the study does not describe a 50 mg/dL condition.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC2766839 (PMC HTML, author manuscript, read in the app's browser; text saved once with get_page_text): abstract, introduction, Methods, Results, Tables 1 and 2, Discussion, acknowledgments, conflict statement, reference list. Figure 2 was viewed as an image and read by eye (approximate values); Figure 1 (concentration curves) was not read. The companion papers on subjective effects and cognitive testing were not read.
